holding: Turning to the question concerning the potential value of the acquired land, we have carefully examined the impugned judgment and note that the High Court, in paragraphs 6 and 7 thereof, has undertaken a detailed analysis of the location and potentiality of the acquired land. The High Court duly considered the nature character of the land, its existing and future utility, its proximity to the main road, educational institutions, petrol pumps, commercial markets, shops, plazas, residential houses, and other relevant factors affecting its market value. re determination of compensation acquisition matters is essentially a question of fact, to be assessed on the basis of relevant material reflecting the market value and potentiality the land at the time of acquisition, and unless such assessment is shown to be based on misreading of evidence, non-consideration material facts or misapplication of any principle of law, this Court would ordinarily not interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by the courts below. &. We find no misreading of evidence, non-consideration material facts or misapplication of any principle of law in the conclusions arrived at by the Referee Court and the High Court so as to warrant interference by this Court. The issue is accordingly answered in the negative. iii. Whether the Referee Court was legally justified in awarding compulsory acquisition charges at the rate of 15% per annum on the compensation the date of notification 4 of the Act until payment, in view of the scope and mandate 23(2) of the Act. 9. As regards the award of 15% per annum on the compensation from the date of Notification 4 of the Act till payment thereof, we find force in the submissions advanced by the learned counsel for the acquiring department. 23(2) of the Act does not contemplate payment of such amount on a recurring annual basis. It is a settled principle of statutory interpretation that where the language of a provision is plain and unambiguous, is bound to give effect to its literal meaning, and cannot read into the provision words, which the legislature has consciously omitted. Moreover, provision 23(2) creates a statutory entitlement of a fixed nature in the form of an additional solatium, which is intended to be compensatory in character and not interest-bearing or time-dependent. The relevant provision is reproduced in relevant part below: $D3. (1) sac cons sunaseesenseniecces tesnaes sed cave vans bewnews coe eeneenercenserion cateengwenses (2) In addition market above provided, the Court shall in every case award a sum of fifteen per centum on such market value, in consideration of the compulsory nature of the acquisition.” A plain reading of the above provision makes it abundantly clear additional of 15% is payable only once on market value determined for the acquired land, as compensation the compulsory nature of the acquisition. The statute does not envisage payment of such amount on a yearly basis. Therefore, the direction of the Referee awarding 15% per annum from the date of notification Section 4 of the Act till payment compensation, which has been maintained by the High Court, is contrary to the express mandate 23(2) of the Act and cannot be sustained. Any such interpretation would rewriting the statute and converting a one-time statutory solatium into a continuing financial liability, which is impermissible in law. The landowners shall, however, be entitled to a one-time payment of 15% on the market value as determined in accordance with law. The issue is answered accordingly. No. 8-P, 9-P, 272 and 293 of 2017 iv. Whether, in view of the amendments made to Section 28 of the Act as applicable in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the landowners were entitled to interest at the rate of 6% per annum on the enhanced compensation awarded by the Referee Court. 10. The claim of the landowners for grant of 6% per annum Section 28 of the Act requires examination in the backdrop legislative changes introduced Province Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Section 28, prior to its amendment by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Land Acquisition (Amendment) Ordinance, 2001, as substituted by the N.-W.F.P. Amendment Ordinance, 1983, read as under: “28. If the sum which, in the opinion of the Court, the Collector ought- to have awarded as compensation is in excess of the sum which the Collector did award as compensation, the award of the Court may direct that the Collector shall pay simple interest on such excess at the rate of six per centum per annum from the date on which he took possession of the land to the date of payment of such excess into Court.” By virtue Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Land Acquisition (Amendment) Ordinance, 2001, aforesaid provision was substituted and now reads as follows: “28. If the sum which, in the opinion of the Court, the Collector ought to have awarded as compensation is in excess of the sum which the Collector did award as compensation, the award of the Court may direct that the Collector shall deposit with the Court such amount as determined by it.” A comparative reading above provisions shows legislature consciously omitted the expression “simple interest” well as the fixed rate of 6% per annum, substituted the same with expression “such determined by it”. legislative intent, therefore, was not to abolish compensatory relief altogether, but, in the backdrop of Aslam Khaki v. Muhammad Hashim (PLD 2000 SC 225), to dispense with the concept of statutory “interest” and the rigidity of a fixed rate, and to confer discretion upon the No. 8-P, 9-P, 272 and 293 of 2017 Referee Court to determine a just and reasonable compensatory amount having regard to the facts of each case. 11. The scope and effect of the amended provision were examined by this in Govt. of KPK v. Misal Khan (2022 SCMR 277), wherein it was held notwithstanding deletion word “interest”, Section 28 retains the jurisdiction of the Court to award an additional over and above the enhanced cover the period between dispossession and actual payment. It was further held that the expression “such as determined by it” is of substantive import and preserves a compensatory head of relief to redress deprivation of property occasioned by delayed payment. 12. The interpretation of the amended provision 28 was again examined further clarified in Govt. of KPK v. Yousaf Khan SCMR 1836), wherein this Court, while affirming compensatory nature 28, held “amount” contemplated therein is essentially “rent” for deprivation of use of land rather than “interest”. It was further held that where evidence of actual fair market rental value is available, the same shall govern determination; however, in absence thereof, a sum equivalent to 6% per annum of the enhanced compensation may be applied as a minimum benchmark of rental value, representing compensatory relief for loss of use. 13. From above pronouncements, following principles clearly emerge: i. the statutory entitlement to 6% interest under the unamended Section 28 no longer survives after the 2001 amendment; :Q: Criminal Original Petitions No. 198 and 199 of 2017 “eee ii. 28, substituted, confers jurisdiction upon Court to determine an additional compensatory over and above the enhanced to cover the period between dispossession and actual payment; iii. such is intended compensate deprivation possession and delayed payment; iv. primary basis is proved market rental land; v. in absence of such evidence, 6% per annum of the enhanced compensation operates as a minimum benchmark of rental value. 14. In the present case, it is not the case of the landowners any evidence was adduced to establish the actual fair market rental acquired for the relevant period. case, therefore, squarely falls within the ratio laid down in the Yousaf Khan’s case. Accordingly, while the landowners are not entitled to claim 6% per annum as interest, they are nevertheless entitled to an additional amount calculated at the rate of 6% per annum of the enhanced compensation, to be treated as minimum compensatory rental value for deprivation of use of land. The issue is answered accordingly. Conclusion: 15. For the foregoing reasons, appeals (C.A. Nos. 8-P & 9-P of 2017) filed by the acquiring are partly allowed to the extent that the direction of the Referee Court, as maintained by the High Court, granting 15% per annum the date of Notification 4 of the Act till payment, is set aside. The landowners shall, however, be entitled to a one-time payment of 15% on the market value determined for the acquired land in terms of Section 23(2) of the Act. However, the determination of market by the Referee Court, as affirmed by the High Court is maintained. No. 8-P, 9-P, 272 and 293 of 2017 - 10: . 16. As regards the appeals (C.A. Nos. 272 & 293 of 2017) filed by the landowners, the same are also partly allowed to the extent that, 28 of the Act, they are held entitled to an additional compensatory amount equivalent to 6% per annum of the enhanced compensation, as minimum rental value, to be computed from the date the Collector took possession of the land till the date of deposit of adjudged into Court. However, their prayer further enhancement of compensation is declined. 17. The appeals are disposed of in the above terms. Nos. 198 and 199 of 2017 18. There are also pending criminal original petitions, wherein landowners have sought initiation of contempt proceedings against the officials of the acquiring department for alleged non-compliance of an interim order passed by this Court during the pendency of the instant appeals. Now that the appeals have been finally decided rights liabilities of the parties have been conclusively determined this judgment, we are of the view that no useful purpose would be served by proceeding further with the contempt petitions or keeping same pending. We, therefore, exercise judicial restraint refrain proceeding further contempt petitions in the facts and circumstances of the case. However, the acquiring department shall forthwith comply with the findings and give effect to the determinations made in this judgment. The amount found payable to the landowners pursuant to this judgment shall be worked out and recovered through the execution proceedings pending before the competent Executing Court. The needful shall be done within three months -1ll1:- . . approaching Executing implementation of this judgment. 19. Accordingly, Nos. 198 and 199 of 2017 are disposed of in the above terms. Appeals filed by both the acquiring and the landowners were dismissed by the High Court through the impugned common judgment, and thereby maintaining adjudged by the Judgment of the Referee Court.

Mere assertions or internal departmental understandings cannot be treated a binding arrangement against landowners, particularly where consequence would be deprivation of their statutory right to seek a reference 18 of the Act.
